questions.q: What is the foundation that every form of MySQL replication is built on?
options: The binary log (binlog) — the same log a standalone server writes for point-in-time recovery
A completely separate subsystem unrelated to backups
SQL Server's transaction log, shared across platforms
The MySQL error log
questions.explain: Replication is a second consumer of the binlog the server was already producing for recovery purposes.

questions.q: What are the three threads involved in traditional MySQL replication, and where do they run?
options: A binlog dump thread on the source, plus an I/O thread and a SQL thread on the replica
Three threads all running on the source server only
A single thread shared between source and replica
Threads named Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary
questions.explain: The binlog dump thread streams from the source; the I/O and SQL threads on the replica pull and apply those events separately.

questions.q: Why does MySQL split the replica side into an I/O thread and a separate SQL thread?
options: So the I/O thread can keep pulling from the source even if applying events is temporarily slower, with the relay log absorbing the difference
To make replication configuration more complicated for no functional reason
Because MySQL requires exactly two threads on every server
The SQL thread and I/O thread do the identical job as a redundancy measure
questions.explain: Splitting pulling from applying means the replica can keep receiving data even during a temporary lag in applying it.

questions.q: What terminology change did MySQL 8.0 complete?
options: "Master/slave" became "source/replica" (e.g. SHOW MASTER STATUS became SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS)
MySQL renamed itself entirely
"Source/replica" was replaced with "master/slave"
There was no terminology change — this is a common misconception
questions.explain: MySQL 8.0 finished a terminology shift from master/slave to source/replica across commands and documentation.

questions.q: If SHOW REPLICA STATUS shows Seconds_Behind_Source climbing steadily, which thread is most likely falling behind?
options: The SQL thread — the I/O thread can keep receiving events into the relay log even while applying lags
The binlog dump thread on the source, which has stopped entirely
There is no way to determine which thread is behind
Both threads always progress at exactly the same rate
questions.explain: Since the I/O thread can pull ahead into the relay log independently, a growing lag typically points to the SQL thread struggling to apply events fast enough.
